name: Buriat
confidence_why: Poppe 1960 (relayed by Walker 1997) and Yamakoshi 2011 describe a weight-sensitive stress on the initial syllable unless a long vowel or diphthong later in the word attracts it, but the experimental work of Budaev 1981 and Bitkeev 1995, followed by Badagarov 2017, finds that standard Khori Buriat has a fixed tonal accent on the last syllable which long vowels do not attract, and Yamakoshi 2003 calls the question unresolved, so the type of the system is under live dispute.

catalog_quote: Another East Mongolian language, Buriat, provides a second example of a rightmost heavy else leftmost pattern with quantity-sensitive nonfinality. The following data are from the same study as that outlined for Khalkha. Findings are consistent with the description of Buriat given by Poppe (1960: 19) and again clarify the interpretation of ‘penultimate’ heavy syllable. Like Khalkha, primary stress falls on the last syllable if it is the only heavy in the word, otherwise on the rightmost nonfinal heavy, otherwise on the initial syllable. Secondary stress falls on heavy syllables and (possibly) the initial syllable when they do not receive primary stress. (33) Buriat Lè L [xa@da] ‘mountain’ Lò Hè [xa$da@˘r] ‘through the mountain’ Hê Hò [bo@˘so$˘] ‘bet, wager’ Lò Hè Hò [da$la@iga$˘r] ‘by sea’ ... Lò Hò Hè Hò [da$la$igaê˘ra$˘] ‘by one’s own sea’ Lò Hê L Hò [xu$da@˘lingda$˘] ‘to the husband’s…
readall_conflicts: For the record, the sources already held by the project disagree among themselves about Buriat: Walker 1997 (citing Poppe 1960:19 as consistent) gives a weight-sensitive rule (final if only heavy, else rightmost nonfinal heavy, else initial); Bertagaev 1968 (Rosetta bxr_phon-1 scan, Russian, garbled scanned, p. 14 of the Yazyki narodov SSSR chapter) says the expiratory stress is weaker than in Mongolian and 'gravitates to a non-initial syllable', with a separate musical stress in optative/imperative forms, vocatives and categorical assertions; the 2026-09-16 check notes Gunzhitova & Dareeva 2020 citing Budaev 1981:107 for tonal stress on the last syllable, and Poppe 1965 sec. 7.22 p. 180 giving a generic Mongolian statement (first syllable unless a later syllable is long). Poppe 1960 itself remains unread.

audit.recode_to: Provisional, pending Budaev 1981 / Poppe 1960:19: mark 'contested'; likely target is weight-insensitive fixed prominence (dynamic initial + final-syllable pitch rise, long vowels not stress-attracting) per Poppe 1938 sec.53, Bertagaev 1968:16, Budaev 1981 apud Badagarov 2017 — rather than 'weight: rightmost nonfinal CVV else initial'.
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: verbatim at the stated place in the Walker 1997 text we hold (pp.27-28). (2) Deciding source: an unpublished 1997 OT typology manuscript; for Buriat it is second-hand (Poppe 1960:19, not yet obtained) plus data 'from the same study' whose only documented recording is of one Khalkha speaker reading Khalkha forms — no Buriat speaker is described anywhere in the ms. Not the best available: Glottolog lists a 340-pp Academy grammar (1962) and Poppe 1960; the Russian literature has a dedicated stress monograph (Budaev 1981) and an experimental study (Bitkeev 1995). (3) Evidence already held by the project cuts against the classification: Poppe 1938 sec.53 (held, read) = expiratory stress always on the first syllable regardless of vowel length, pitch rise on the final syllable, long non-initial vowels merely sound stronger; Bertagaev 1968:16 (held scanned, decoded) = weak stress tending to a non-initial syllable
audit.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again.— agree: lines 1431-1451 (footer p.27) carry the record's passage verbatim ('Another East Mongolian language, Buriat.. rightmost nonfinal heavy, otherwise on the initial syllable. Secondary stress falls on heavy syllables and (possibly) the initial syllable'), ex.(33) continues to p.28 (lines 1454-1500) and the 'Khalkha and Buriat words.. L H H L' distributivity note is at lines 1516-1526, matching loc. Provenance caveat also verified: fn.5 (lines 1275-1280) documents only 'recordings.. of the Khalkha forms as read by a native speaker of Khalkha Mongol

sources.citation: Badagarov, Zhargal B. 2017. O tipakh slovesnogo udareniya v mongol'skikh yazykakh [Word-stress patterns in Mongolic languages]. Vestnik Kalmytskogo instituta gumanitarnykh issledovanij RAN 34(6): 111-116. DOI 10.22162/2075-7794-2017-34-6-111-116.
sources.quote: Distinguishes a Khalkha type (pitch accent shifts onto the first long vowel) from a 'Buryat-Oirat type' characterised by 'a constant position of the accent on the last syllable', tonal/musical in nature [Budaev 1981: 97, 104, 108]; long vowels do not pull the pitch rise onto themselves and an unaccented long vowel becomes overlong, e.g. bur. хаагаа [хаааˈгаа], ооһороо [оооһъˈроо]; Khori Buryat (standard base) is 'close to Kalmyk' in accent, Zakamensk Buryat close to Khalkha. Also reports Bitkeev 1995:83 (experimental, Kalmyk and Buryat): main 'qualitative' stress = clear first-syllable vowel,
sources.note: Open-access synthesis by a Buryat State University Mongolist placing Khori Buryat in a 'final tonal accent, long vowels do not attract' type and summarising Budaev 1981 and Bitkeev 1995; downloaded now, directly contradicts the record.

sources.citation: Yamakoshi, Yasuhiro. 2011. Shinekhen Buryat. In Y. Yamakoshi (ed.), Grammatical Sketches from the Field, 137-177. Tokyo: ILCAA, Tokyo University of Foreign Studies.
sources.quote: 'Shinekhen Buryat has two accent systems: pitch accent and stress accent. Both systems are phonologically indistinctive, and clitics are not accentuated. a. Stress accent: The initial syllable is stressed. If VV (long vowel or diphthong) are found in other syllables, the syllable that has VV is stressed. E.g. xorgan "lamb", temeen "camel", gasjoon "bitter". b. Pitch accent: VN of the last syllable are pitched higher.' No rule for words with several VV. Variety is Shinekhen (Khori/Aga emigrant Buryat in China; Glottolog lists China Buriat as a separate languoid).

sources.citation: Абаева, Ю. Д. 2020. Диалектный корпус как средство сохранения и изучения бурятской просодии [A dialect corpus as a means of preserving and studying Buryat prosody]. Томский журнал лингвистических и антропологических исследований 3(29): 9-19.
sources.note: States that Buryat suprasegmentals have been studied instrumentally only for the literary language and that dialect prosody (stress, intonation) is undescribed apart from impressionistic notes; describes a spoken dialect corpus with Praat measurement of F0, intensity and duration and a prosodic transcription marking accent contours (rising/falling/level) and H/M/L pitch levels at utterance start, nucleus and end. No claim of lexical tone; no word-accent analysis in this paper.

tone.quote: §1 посвящен исследованию интонации побудительных высказываний в бурятском языке. В категорическом побуждении, выраженном глаголом в форме повелительно-желательного наклонения, движение основного тона нисходящее- Или восходяще-нисходящее. Частотный диапазон как повышения, так и понижения не превышает 5-7 пт. Регистровый уровень всей фразы - высокий. … Просодические особенности слов выражаются в небольшом повышении мелодики к концу слова на 1-5 пт.
tone.locator: Avtoreferat, 'Osnovnoe soderzhanie raboty', Glava II par.1 (Buryat); HTML unpaginated
tone.translation: Par. 1 is devoted to the intonation of imperative utterances in Buryat. In a categorical imperative expressed by a verb in the imperative-optative mood, the movement of the fundamental tone is falling or rising-falling. The frequency range of both the rise and the fall does not exceed 5-7 semitones. The register level of the whole phrase is high. … The prosodic features of words are expressed in a small rise of the melody towards the end of the word, by 1-5 semitones.
tone.summary: Instrumental study of sentence intonation: F0 contours (in semitones), register, tempo and intensity of Buryat imperative utterances; pitch treated only as intonation, nothing said about lexical tone.

tone.says: Experimental (oscillographic) study of sentence rhythm and F0 melody of simple Buryat sentences; sentence-level prosody, not lexical tone. Relevant because, per Budaev 1984, Buryat word accent and sentence melody are both carried by F0 and must be disentangled; what the book itself says about word-level pitch was not seen.

sources.note: Experimental (articulatory) monograph on the Buryat vowel and consonant inventory. Per Budaev's 1984 avtoreferat it is 'one of the first experimental works on Buryat phonetics' and at p. 190 it specifically stressed the need to study Buryat accentuation by objective methods; it does not itself analyse word stress or pitch (no accent chapter reported). Text not seen.
